rationale: The Meridian Review is an independent long-form culture publication. The direction is unapologetically print-derived: a high-contrast serif display, a warm ivory stock, and a single ink-red for editorial marks. Layout gives text room to be read slowly. Color is nearly absent by design — the writing is the design.

palette.semantic: Ink black — headlines, rules, and body text; the publication's dominant mark.
Warm grey — bylines, standfirsts, and secondary editorial furniture.
Editorial red — section marks, pull-quote rules, and drop caps; used sparingly for emphasis.
Ivory stock — the page; warm and low-glare for long reading.
Ink black body text at book contrast on ivory.
Faded grey — folios, timestamps, and caption credits.

typography.semantic: A high-contrast Didone serif — the front-of-book display face; dramatic at large sizes.
A readable transitional serif for long-form body — comfortable at book measure and small leading.
A neutral grotesque, small and tracked, to contrast the serifs on captions and standfirsts.

layout.semantic: A narrow, centered measure of roughly 66 characters — optimized for sustained reading, not scanning.
A wide, indented pull quote in the display serif with an editorial-red rule, breaking the column rhythm.

cohesion.summary: Highly cohesive through restraint: two serifs and one grotesque on a single ivory stock, with red as the lone chromatic mark. The system reads as one continuous publication.

principles.title: The measure is sacred
principles.detail: Body text never exceeds ~66 characters per line; readability outranks filling the viewport.

principles.title: Red is punctuation, not paint
principles.detail: Editorial red marks structure — section breaks, drop caps, pull-quote rules — and is never used as a fill or background.

principles.title: Serif carries the voice
principles.detail: Display and body are both serif; the lone grotesque exists only to set captions apart, keeping the literary register intact.
